title: Median
body:
Sort the data and take the middle value. With an even $n$ there are two middles, so average them.
The median is the 50th percentile: half the data sits below it and half above, by definition.

**Its point is robustness.** Moving any value on one side of the median, however far, does not move
the median at all, because only the ordering matters and not the magnitudes. That makes it the
right centre for skewed data (incomes, house prices, response times) and for data with outliers or
open-ended top categories, where the [[Mean]] is either misleading or not computable.

The trade is that it throws away information. It uses the ranks and ignores the values, so it is a
worse estimator when the data really is symmetric and clean, and it does not lead anywhere: no
[[Central Limit Theorem]] as clean as the mean's, no closed-form algebra, no [[Variance]]
decomposition. That is why the inference half of [[STATISTICS]] is built on $\bar{x}$ despite the
median being the better summary in many real datasets.

The median is also the value $c$ minimising $\sum|x_i - c|$, the absolute-deviation version of the
[[Mean]]'s least squares property. Same reason $L_1$ regression is robust and $L_2$ is not, which
[[Vector Norm]] in Linear Algebra for Data Science states from the other end.

It generalises to **quartiles** ($Q_1$, $Q_2 = $ median, $Q_3$) and percentiles, and
$\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$ is the robust spread that pairs with it. A [[Descriptive Statistics|boxplot]]
is a drawing of exactly these five numbers.
